Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Wednesday, 16 October 2024 at 12 noon
(Day 056)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu SC and
Ms Emily Aitken for NSW Health
Mr Scott Chapman for Dr Michael Bonning

THE COMMISSIONER: Good afternoon.
MR MUSTON: The first panel of witnesses we have today are
both from Advanced Pharmacy Australia.
A copy of the statement that they have prepared,
Commissioner, you will find behind tab L13, it is
exhibit L13.
THE COMMISSIONER: I have that, thanks.
MR MUSTON: Starting on your left is Jerry Yik, and next
to him is Jonathan Penm. I think Mr Yik will take an
affirmation and Mr Penm will take an oath.
<JERRY YIK, affirmed: [12.01pm]
<JONATHAN PENM, sworn:
MR MUSTON: Starting with you, Mr Yik, would you state
your full name for the record, please.
MR YIK: Yes, my name is Mr Jerry Yik.
MR MUSTON: You are the head of policy and advocacy at
Advanced Pharmacy Australia?
MR YIK: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Mr Penm, could you state your full name for
the record, please.
DR PENM: Yes, I'm Jonathan Penm.
MR MUSTON: You are the vice chair of the New South Wales
branch committee of Advanced Pharmacy Australia?
DR PENM: Correct.
MR MUSTON: Also a member of the faculty pharmacy of the
University of Sydney.
THE COMMISSIONER: Is it Dr Penm?
DR PENM: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Dr Penm.

You have both prepared a statement dated 26 September
2024 to assist the Inquiry with its work. Do you have
a copy of that with you?
MR YIK: I do, yes.
DR PENM: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Have you each had an opportunity to review it
before giving your evidence today?
MR YIK: Yes.
DR PENM: We have.
MR MUSTON: Are you satisfied, to the best of your
knowledge, that its contents are true and correct?
MR YIK: Yes.
DR PENM: Yes.
MR MUSTON: That will form part of the tender in due
course.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Can I take you to page 4 of your statement
where you set out for us a number of key issues. In fact
before going to that, could I ask you for the benefit of we
laypeople just to explain the typical role of a hospital
pharmacist within a public hospital setting?
MR YIK: Yes, sure. Hospital pharmacists are very, very
important to the supply of medicines to patients in
hospitals, all the way from the - upon entry into hospital,
where we might be in the emergency department, all the way
through to your entire inpatient journey, upon discharge
from hospital, and then as well as any community care that
might be provided or any transitions of care services that
might be provided as well.
Now, supply of medicines is a core part of what
pharmacists do. As we all might be very familiar with, we
tend to see pharmacists as the people that give us our
medicines. That is very, very true and that is a very

important task where various checks are required to make
sure that you've got the right patient, the right medicine,
the right dosage, the right route of administration, so
that nothing goes wrong with the medicine that you take.
MR MUSTON: Pausing there, to the extent that we might all
understand if you are an outpatient or an inpatient within
a hospital and a doctor prescribes a particular medication,
the hospital pharmacist will receive that prescription,
probably electronically these days, and collect and
administer - distribute whatever the product is?
MR YIK: Yes, that's right. What you have described there
is a fairly reactive model, so the pharmacist is at the
very end reviewing everything, and what - but in the acute
setting, what is best practice, as described in our
standards, is that you actually have pharmacists embedded
in the wards providing bedside medication management
services where you can actually review the medication
chart, make sure that the prescribing or charting of that
medicine is safe and appropriate for the patient before the
nurse then orders that medicine.
The pharmacist should be involved in that prescribing
and charting process alongside the doctor so that even
before it makes it down to the dispensary for the
pharmacist to supply it, it's already been deemed to be
a safe and appropriate prescription for that patient. So
that is probably the more clinical and cognitive service
that should be provided and what hospital pharmacists
should be able to provide, and which is, you know, an
extremely value-adding area.
MR MUSTON: Going back to the point of admission, we've
heard some evidence and heard some discussion on some of
our regional trips about medication reconciliation as
a role that pharmacists have within a hospital setting.
Could you just explain to us, say from the perspective of
a hypothetical patient who enters the hospital system, what
that involves?
MR YIK: Yes. I think yes, medication reconciliation is
an activity that requires pharmacists to undertake
a history of what medicines that patient is on prior to
entering hospital, so that when they are admitted, they can
have all their regular medicines from home being charted
and/or their reason for admission to hospital might be

medication related as well. So this has actually been, you
know, a subject across various inquiries in New South
Wales, but a typical patient in a hospital might take
anywhere from 2 to 5 to 10 medicines depending upon the
patient profile. In that medicine profile there might be
some medicines that are very, very appropriate for the
patient but, at some point, there might have been an
unintentional overdose, there might have been a doubling up
of some medicines because a patient hasn't had a review for
a while.
So they might come into hospital and be taking the
wrong medicines and the pharmacist who does the medication
reconciliation can find that out. But even if there's
nothing wrong with the patient's medicines, there is still
a duty of the hospital to make sure the patient is taking
the medicines that they were on prior to home.
So if you're a patient that's using something to lower
your blood pressure, something to lower your cholesterol,
taking an anti-depressant, some pain medicines as well, you
should expect that in your five-day inpatient stay, that
you should have access to those medicines as well and
continue that therapy. You shouldn't have to stop taking
those medicines for five or six days while you are in
hospital. And to make sure that pharmacists and the
hospital can provide the right medicines, that's where that
medication reconciliation occurs, to make sure that we are
taking an accurate medication history, because if it's not
done, then the patient goes without medicines or, worse,
might be prescribed the wrong medicines.
MR MUSTON: When you say "prescribed the wrong medicines",
do you mean prescribed something which is inconsistent with
or reacts adversely with something that the patient is or
has been taking?
MR YIK: So it could be they are prescribed the wrong
medicine or the wrong dosage compared to what they were on
at home and, yes, it has potential to be one that they
might have an adverse reaction to. Why that might occur
sometimes is if you don't have a pharmacist doing the
medication reconciliation - and evidence proves and
suggests that pharmacists are the best clinicians to do
a medication history for medication reconciliation - where
you rely upon a doctor or a nurse who has a lot of other
things to do to take a really basic medication

reconciliation that's not comprehensive and may not be
entirely accurate, then charting and prescribing decisions
made on those types of medication reconciliation activities
by nurses and doctors can lead to some discrepancies and
errors.
So without a pharmacist doing a really comprehensive
and accurate medication reconciliation, that's what might
precipitate the issues that you have described.
MR MUSTON: You refer to a "comprehensive and accurate
reconciliation". What, in a practical sense, does that
involve beyond asking a patient to the extent that they are
capable of responding, "What are you taking"?
MR YIK: Many activities - and as you said, it's not just
asking the patient and as we know unfortunately patients,
certainly when they are in the acute environment, can be
poor historians. So we have to make sure we are checking
other sources. That could include the My Health Record;
could be calling up their usual community pharmacies as
well to look for dispensing records, and that might - and
some patients might have more than one pharmacy, which
makes it more complicated; contacting their prescribers as
well, so their GP or GP practice; any specialists as well
that they might have; carers as well. Yes, so there is
a variety of sources that we can use to get that accurate
medication history and often we do need to do that. But as
you can imagine, that's quite a significant amount of time
to do an accurate and comprehensive medication history that
you just would not expect a nurse or a doctor to do.
MR MUSTON: That would obviously require a sufficient
workforce within a pharmacy department to be performing
that task in relation to patients as they come in to the
facility.
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. You require pharmacists to be
staffed on all those wards, especially in general medicine
wards, in emergency medicine where you are getting the high
flow of patients, to do that medication history.
Unfortunately, there are many, many, I would probably say
the vast majority of New South Wales hospital pharmacy
departments and their wards won't have a continual and
regular clinical pharmacist service at those wards.
MR MUSTON: In relation to that reconciliation process,

would it be right to assume that there's a spectrum in
terms of the rigour that one needs to apply to that task
depending on the nature of the patient and the reason for
their presentation? So, for example, if a fit and well
patient turned up to have some stitches put in to a gash on
their arm and was going to be prescribed some painkillers
to go away from the emergency department with, you would
probably not need to be quite as rigorous in terms of your
reconciliation, as, for example, an aged care facility
patient who comes in with a mystery bag of foil tablets
and --
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. I think we always obviously
apply risk assessments and we provide our services on
a risk-based approach, so looking at patient profiles, and
that could be age-related factors, can be their medical
history, can be the number of medicines that they are on.
It can be the types of medicines that they are on. There
are many patients who are taking 15, 20 medicines, and they
can be completely appropriate, but you might have patients
who are only taking five and they are all inappropriate or
can have the propensity to cause an adverse reaction.
So we aim to provide medication review to every single
patient. There is no way that is occurring in New South
Wales based on the funding issues that we've explored, and
even applying a risk-based approach and even trying to
ensure that we only review our high-risk patients, even
that service level is not able to be met in New South Wales
in many, many departments.
MR MUSTON: When you say it is not able to be met for
funding reasons, are you essentially telling us that there
are insufficient hospital pharmacists employed within
facilities to enable that process to be undertaken with
respect to the patients that, at least in the view of
pharmacists, it ought to be undertaken in relation to?
MR YIK: Yes, I am. So as we present in our evidence, the
number of hospital pharmacists in New South Wales is - you
know, comparatively speaking to Victoria and Queensland,
when you're looking at the number of hospital pharmacists
to the number of hospital beds that you have, New South
Wales is far, far behind.
So in that scenario, how do we - how do New South
Wales pharmacy departments apportion their pharmacists and

their workforce to the services that they have to provide?
Unfortunately, a lot of them can't put pharmacists on to
the wards providing those clinical and cognitive services
and preventing medication errors from occurring, preventing
prescribing errors from occurring. Where they are being
forced to provide most of the services is at the very tail
end of - simply because we only have so many pharmacists,
we have to focus all our efforts on the supply of medicines
and it's only when they are asked to supply medicine, they
receive a prescription and we find out, "Hold on, there are
errors here. Why has this been allowed to go on for X
number of days when it should have been detected at the
very beginning?"
Best practice dictates that you detect these errors at
the very beginning, as other states are able to do because
they do have enough workforce, but in New South Wales, in
many areas, that error may only be detected at the very end
when the pharmacist is asked to supply that medicine, if at
all.
THE COMMISSIONER: The ratios that you have given in the
table on page 2 - any questions I ask, and also this
applies to Mr Muston, both of you should feel free to chip
in and answer if you want to - why is New South Wales so
much different to Victoria and Queensland? Funding might
be one issue, but are there any other reasons that you're
aware of?
MR YIK: Look, I think funding is a - it probably comes
down to funding, at the end of the day. I think there are
other areas around workforce investment as well, so there
is a workforce shortage across not just healthcare sectors
but every sector at the moment but historically, New South
Wales hospital pharmacy departments have been underfunded.
We aren't funding enough internships for pharmacy students
to come into the hospital setting. We know that hospital -
the hospital setting is the most desirable setting for
pharmacy students, but I think New South Wales currently
only offers 40-odd, according to our submission.
In Victoria, we've got over 100. So if you are only
getting 40 new interns each year and you want them to
continue, then you've got a fairly limited pool. So
I think funding is probably what it comes down to.
Recognition from the LHDs about what pharmacy departments
provide and the services that they provide and providing

requisite funding, that's a conversation that we hear from
various hospitals and pharmacy departments is - it's
probably not taken seriously. So our pharmacy departments
are asked to do --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, what is not taken seriously?
MR YIK: A lot of our pharmacy departments are asked to do
a lot of extra activities to respond to the needs of the
state healthcare system. We're like, of course, we want to
do that, we want to make sure that we're providing the best
care possible but when we then say, "Well, we're going to
need this amount of pharmacy technicians, this amount of
pharmacists", the response from various levels within the
ministry or the LHD is that, "Well, sorry, we can't. We
can't fund that. You're just going to have to make that
happen", and so that's when it comes to, "Well, what can we
cut or what can we rearrange?" And I was speaking to
someone who was job was rearranged at some point during his
career due to these funding decisions.
DR PENM: I would just quickly add to it. We have lots of
people wanting to work in hospital. We just don't have
enough positions for them to have. And then those that are
in there, the pay structure doesn't reward them for their
contribution. When you're talking about the restructuring,
we often get those requests that say this hospital is
implementing a new service, implementing more emergency
department beds, implementing more wards. They will tell
us how amazing those new facilities are, the new doctors
they will hire for it, the new nurses they will hire for
it. But in the pharmacy, we go, "So, are we getting
anything?" "No". Pharmacy is generally not considered
when it comes to new services and we've just been taking
that load on and on and on and we've just got to this point
now that our ratios just seem vastly lower than other
states.
THE COMMISSIONER: By having the one to eight hospital bed
ratio in Victoria and Queensland as distinct from one to 13
in New South Wales metro and then the one to 18, one to 14
versus one to 27 for regional hospitals, what are the
consequences you think for having - in relation to the
different ratios? In other words, what different services
are able to be provided in the metro or regional hospitals
in Victoria or Queensland that can't be provided in
New South Wales because of those ratios, and what risks are

being mollified in those other states that aren't in
New South Wales because of those ratios?
MR YIK: As I described earlier, it probably comes down to
the ability to provide clinical pharmacy services at the
ward.
THE COMMISSIONER: On the ward.
MR YIK: Yes, on the ward. So say you've got a junior
doctor who wants to chart a medicine for a patient and they
want to find out, well, is this the correct dose given this
patient's renal function, where is a pharmacist to ask that
question? In other states, you will have a pharmacist who
is there, that can provide that junior doctor some advice
on that. In New South Wales, there isn't, and so that
error or - is then detected at the end.
THE COMMISSIONER: Potential error.
MR YIK: The potential error is then potentially detected
by the pharmacist at the very end, if they're asked to
supply that medicine.
DR PENM: We do have some evidence for that on page 11
where we talk about the partnered pharmacist medication
charting model. That is a model that is implemented in the
other states because they have the pharmacists to deliver
that service. That's just an extension of what Mr Yik
talked about with pharmacists --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, this is what you call the PPMC?
DR PENM: That's correct. So once the pharmacist does the
medication reconciliation, the pharmacist then charts those
medications, because they have the time and the ability to
do so, and they have done the medication reconciliation
because they have the staff to do so, and they show by
doing that they have now reduced that length of stay by
10 per cent, they have reduced the errors per patient by
62.4 per cent. That's a service that you can only do if
you have the staffing to do it.
THE COMMISSIONER: Sure.
MR YIK: That's a really good example again of where our
pharmacy departments are being asked to do more but without

the resources to do that. So that PPMC program, we gave
evidence on that at the ramping inquiry, and we're really
grateful to the New South Wales Government for accepting
that recommendation and putting it into the report.
The status of that is the Ministry of Health is
progressing this program and they have put out - we
understand that they have put out an EOI to various
hospitals and LHDs to ask, "Who wants to participate?"
There is lots of interest from many, many LHDs but what we
understand is they have also been told there won't be any
additional money to fund this service.
THE COMMISSIONER: So this is recommendation 8?
MR YIK: In the ramping inquiry?
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR YIK: Yes, that's right.
THE COMMISSIONER: We find that - do you have your whole
statement?
MR YIK: Yes, I do, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: So this is the New South Wales
Government response to the ramping inquiry, just call it
that, page 5 --
MR YIK: So they've accepted that.
THE COMMISSIONER: -- that the New South Wales Government
will provide funding to increase the number of hospital
pharmacists so that their availability better matches
operating hours, et cetera. That's supported in principle.
MR YIK: Yes, and we are still waiting for that
investment. But the PPMC is just one of many different,
you know, additional requirements or initiatives that we
all want to do for the benefits of New South Wales
patients, but we keep being told continually that there is
no extra funding to provide that.
MR MUSTON: Just to pick up on something, Mr Yik, you said
a bit earlier, the position in many facilities is, if I've
understood you correctly, that the pharmacy workforce that

is employed is effectively detained full time keeping up
with the distribution of medication from the pharmacy
department in response to prescriptions that come down from
the wards.
MR YIK: Yes. I would say so, that the core service of
a pharmacist is to supply medicines and, you know, their
role in the hospitals is to make sure that patients receive
medicines. That's a really, really important part of what
we do. But in an environment where we are meeting our own
professional standards, we are not just supplying
medicines, we are also making sure that the charting and
prescribing of those medicines is safe and appropriate
before it even reaches the pharmacy to dispense
a prescription.
So we should be detecting the errors or assessing it
for its appropriateness as early as possible, not at the
very end when we are in the basement, when we don't have
access to the nurse or the doctor to get things changed.
MR MUSTON: Just working through this hypothetical
patient, if we put to one side the workforce challenges and
assume the hypothetical patient appears at a hospital that
has a hypothetical workforce where pharmacists can provide
the best level of service you think they're able to
provide, it starts with a thorough reconciliation of their
existing medication. In relation to that, is that a task
that can usually be performed by a relatively junior
pharmacist, not wanting to downplay the importance of it,
but --
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. These are, you know, key
competencies for pharmacists and certainly undertaking
medication reconciliation, medication histories, is
something that we train students and interns to do as well
so that once they are registered, they are more than
competent to do that independently.
I might throw to Dr Penm, who actually trains students
and interns who do these activities.
DR PENM: Yes, so we've got some data from
Sydney University showing that pharmacy students, pharmacy
interns, pharmacists, all of them are able to do it, and
they do in a way that is more accurate than doctors and
nurses. That's not to downplay their knowledge base; it

just shows that we have a different focus when we do it and
we are particularly conscious of things around strengths,
formulations, things that we see every day, and we know
that doctors and nurses have other things that they need to
prioritise and they don't see. It's a core competency,
something that the more junior workforce can do.
I will also just talk to your point about how do we
provide that value. When we're doing these tasks, it's
often obvious to us that if you solve the problem at the
beginning, it saves a lot of problems at the end.
So when we had that reactive model Mr Yik was talking
about earlier, we were just identifying that a lot of the
problems could have been sorted out much quicker, much
faster if a pharmacist was involved, which is why we have
become involved earlier, and that then speaks to the point
on page 9 that every dollar spent on pharmacy comes to $23
of savings, because the kinds of things we're fixing are
actually easy to be fixed at the beginning versus trying to
fix them at the end.
MR MUSTON: So working through that process, obviously
money spent on a thorough reconciliation of someone's
medication has the potential to produce better or quicker
or at least less adverse outcomes, which has a financial
benefit attached to it. What is the next role for
a well-provisioned pharmacy department in terms of the
journey of this hypothetical patient who has been admitted?
You have completed your reconciliation of their medication,
they're receiving some medical treatment or a medical
assessment is being made of them by a doctor - what's the
pharmacist's role there?
MR YIK: I guess inpatients is probably the next, you
know, journey for that patient, and so as an inpatient,
depending on what you are diagnosed with, it could be - you
are likely to be prescribed some new medicines, they could
be - just say you have got an infection that is really
resistant to a lot of anti-microbials, so even choosing the
right anti-microbial, making sure that's at the right dose
for you, that any all your issues - that any adverse
affects are addressed and detected appropriately as well,
interpreting your cultures and sensitivity testings to
guide anti-microbial selection, looking at your renal and
hepatic function as well to inform the dosing of that
medicine, making sure that medicine is compounded correctly

as well by the pharmacy department, and making sure the
nurse knows how to administer that medicine appropriately,
whether that be by infusion or injection, because again,
even the administration can cause issues as well.
So I guess there's a lot of - for that inpatient, it's
any changes to their medicines, be it a new medication
being charted, an old medicine being ceased or withdrawn
because that's causing harm or has the propensity to cause
harm, and any other additional medicines to treat side
effects, such as nausea, vomiting, pain - all these things
require a pharmacist to review daily and to inform the
charting and prescribing of those medicines as well.
MR MUSTON: And so that presumably is a role that would be
done collaboratively with the doctor who is treating the
patient?
MR YIK: That's right.
MR MUSTON: What is the extra that the pharmacist brings
to that collaboration that one might not ordinarily expect
of a doctor who is treating the patient?
MR YIK: So there is a lot of - because the patient's
health and their status in the acute setting is changing
continually, it does require extra focus on the medicines
to make sure that those medicines and the dosages are
appropriate for the patient, because the next day your
patient might be having acute renal failure and that would
require review of all the medicines to make sure that those
medicines aren't going to make that worse.
We also recognise that a lot of the prescribing and
charting in the hospital setting is done by junior doctors
who are less experienced with charting and prescribing of
medicines as well, and so having a pharmacist who is a bit
more experienced around the medicines can really improve
the quality and accuracy of prescribing as well.
Charting of medicines on a medication chart, it's not
just writing down the drug and the dose. There are also
other - that you're getting the mode of administration
right, any variable dosing issues as well, having to get
that right as well. Annotating, you know, making sure any
medication orders that might need to be withheld because
a patient has a procedure the next day or in the next two

days. I guess there's a lot more - the patients aren't in
a stable setting, their health status isn't stable, and so
there's a lot of factors that go into the safe and quality
prescribing of medicines that requires a lot more attention
than, say, when you do have a stable patient in a community
setting.
DR PENM: I'll just add, there are at least two other main
things to focus on where pharmacists do provide value. One
is we do a lot more training on medications. Our knowledge
of medications is vaster because of that, but we have
a very generalist view. So, for instance, say
a cardiologist - cardiologists will know all their
cardiology medications very well, but they might not know
the psychiatric medicines as well. A pharmacist will be
aware that, "Actually, that has a lot of side effects, so
they need to be monitored; they interact." So it is
a really good partnership. Doctors will know what is best
to treat them in front of them, and we know whether it does
actually fit within the context of the patient, from that
broader perspective. That's often the types of issues that
we identify - drug interactions that we identify - earlier
on.
Another part of it is just that pharmacy sees things.
We really like the detail. We love about - the doses
matter to us. The formulations really, really matter,
getting the right dose for a patient with renal impairment,
that gets us excited. We want to make sure they get the
right dose, and that's often not the things that get
doctors excited. They have a lot of other things that get
them excited and they can do it, they're capable of doing
it, but they're just not high priority tasks and they get
skipped, they get missed.
That's where the errors happen because it is hard to
do tasks that you don't like to do. I know that's
a generalisation, but generally, pharmacy really enjoys
making medication safety a priority, we really like to do
that, we do it well because of that. So it's just a really
good partnership, and that is constantly seen when we ask
doctors, "Do you like having a pharmacist?" They go, "We
love it, they do the stuff I don't want to do and they do
it well." And pharmacy go, "And we love doing it". So to
just not have that combination, it seems like you're just
missing out.

MR YIK: And to make sure we are not putting our doctors
in disrepute, it is not that they don't like doing it --
THE COMMISSIONER: I didn't assume that.
MR YIK: But it's also they --
THE COMMISSIONER: The lack of excitement only means that
they're happy for you to do it.
MR YIK: They don't have the time to do it as well. They
also just don't have the time to do it as well. A lot of
junior doctors, certainly from other states, they have been
brought up in a system where they do have a pharmacist that
does a lot of these things for them and then they come to
New South Wales and go, "Where is the pharmacist?"
DR PENM: I think the PPMC model that we talked about
earlier highlights that, that all the medical profession
really enjoy us doing that task. They actually say "This
is great".
MR MUSTON: You tell us a little bit in your statement
about the advanced skills training for pharmacists in the
various different strands of advanced skills that
pharmacists can pursue. Presumably where a pharmacist has
obtained some advanced skill training and experience in a
particular area, whether it be, you know, chemotherapy
medication or any of the other wide array of advanced
skills that you have identified by reference to those nice
little icons in your statement, that pharmacist will be
able to bring a particular degree of skill and experience
to the table when dealing with issues like this, and
perhaps significantly more than a junior doctor, who is
just starting on their professional journey.
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. I think what Dr Penm's talked
about, us being specialists but also generalists, is
a really good example, because say you're in a psychiatry
ward, you've got the psychiatry consultant and the
registrar, who might be really laser focused on the
psychiatry medicines, and rightly they should be, but the
pharmacist will also take that holistic view and look at,
well, how does it impact their medicines for their
cholesterol, how does it impact their medicines for their
blood pressure?

These are all important factors for us to all
consider, so the pharmacist will take that viewpoint in
there. I think you are right about the need for advanced
skills and specialisation as well. What we do know with
health care is that patients are coming into hospital more
unwell, more advanced in their disease state and so that
also then requires your practitioners, including your
pharmacists, to make sure that they have the right skills
to provide care for these patients. So we do try to
specialise pharmacists where we can. If you've got an
oncology ward in New South Wales or a psychiatry ward in
New South Wales, you don't just put every pharmacist -
sorry, any pharmacist in that ward; you want to make sure
that the pharmacist you're putting into that ward already
has the skills in oncology, in psychiatry, so that they're
providing the best and safest and highest quality health
care to that patient wherever possible. That's not being
done at the moment in many parts of New South Wales, but
it's certainly what patients should be expecting from us.
MR MUSTON: So in terms of those forms of advanced
training, in smaller regional and rural facilities which
offer a general array of services to their patients,
obviously whilst a pharmacist might choose to pursue some
advanced training, the real skill that they bring to bear
in that setting is going to be that slightly more general
skill set; would that be right?
MR YIK: Yes, that's right. I think there are some -
you'll have general pharmacists and general medicine
pharmacists in all hospitals, whether it be rural, regional
or metropolitan areas, but I think that there is going to
be more and more demands from patients to have specialist
services outside of metropolitan areas.
Around the country, there is a need for this as well.
We are ready, our workforce, to provide the services
through different models of care. So be that outreach or
telehealth or remote services, these can be provided and
these will only proliferate even more in the coming years.
MR MUSTON: Just in relation to that, dealing, for
example, with cancer treatment and the delivery of
chemotherapy to people closer to where they live, is there
scope for a well-provisioned pharmacy workforce to enhance
in any way the ability to deliver, in perhaps more regional
and remote settings, treatment of that type to patients

where you might not actually have an on-the-ground
workforce that's well experienced and skilled in the
delivery of that type of care, the chemotherapy kind of
care?
MR YIK: Look, that is progressing and that has been
rolled out, certainly in WA for a telehealth chemotherapy
service. In New South Wales there is the Virtual Clinical
Pharmacy Service, or VCPS, that has actually won a few
awards, where they are providing pharmacy services to
patients electronically and via telehealth.
At the outset, it is important for us to state that
in-person services are of the highest quality, but because
of the workforce shortage, a lot of hospitals have been
forced to look at providing services digitally and via
telehealth means, and that has bridged a massive access gap
in access to pharmacists, pharmacist services, the Med Rec
counselling by a pharmacist, where it otherwise would
simply just not have been provided at all due to funding or
due to not having a pharmacist living in the area. So
these means have now bridged that gap and some of these
cancer services, you now can actually have an oncology
pharmacist speak to a cancer patient, look at the
medication chart, making sure that that oncology medicine
is charted appropriately, it's the right dose, it's
calculated appropriately, before it's then compounded and
administered to the patient.
MR MUSTON: Continuing to walk through this hypothetical
patient's journey, decisions around prescribing are dealt
with collaboratively in an ideal situation, charting is
then done by a pharmacist in the ideal situation. Pausing
there, I'm assuming that having regard to the competing
pressures on doctors' times, that, to be blunt, having
a pharmacist deal with things like the charting is a more
cost effective way of dealing with that problem from the
system's point of view, than having the doctor do that?
Would that be a fair assumption?
DR PENM: It's not just cost effective; it's more accurate
and safer.
MR MUSTON: Better in almost every respect?
DR PENM: Best practice.

MR YIK: The evidence that we've provided, it's been
evaluated multiple times and it's been shown to reduce the
admission length because the administering is more
accurate. There's dramatic reduction in the errors as
well, and the qualitative feedback that we've got from
doctors, from a variety of states, is that they have more
time to spend with patients and to do other things. So
where you have a pharmacist taking over a lot of that
charting, it just - it's quite a big relief to a lot of the
doctors involved.
MR MUSTON: In this hypothetical well-resourced facility
where the patient is discharged, what's the pharmacist's
role at the point of discharge if they have one?
DR PENM: Yes, so we know discharge and transitions of
care is a high-risk scenario. A lot of medication-related
harm happens at transitions of care, and some of these
patients come back to hospital. That happens for a variety
of reasons: one, it's not just the clinical decisions that
are being made, what's best for them, but there's a lot of
coordination to make sure that the primary care, both
physician and community pharmacy, are aware of what's
happening and that those medicines are actually available
outside and they can do it in a timely manner.
Within New South Wales, we're not part of the
pharmaceutical benefits reform and so we don't have access
to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme medication quantities
that all the other states in Australia do, so we generally
discharge patients with about five to seven days' worth,
and that means that they've got to see their GP in that
short amount of time to get more medicines, otherwise they
just go without until they do. That's part of it.
We've got the clinical decisions, that the right
medicines are prescribed, the labs have all been monitored,
they're not getting side effects from those, they're
getting the right response.
Then we've got to coordinate that everyone knows what
they should be on, including the patient. That often -
well, not often but can sometimes be missed, and then that
comes with patient education, counselling, producing
patient medication lists, so it's also written down,
because we know, no matter how much I tell you, you're not
going to remember everything, and that applies to all of

us.
It just takes time to do all of those things, and
without pharmacists, it doesn't happen. That's why
transitions of care is such a high-risk area, it is
considered a priority area, the Australian Commission have
already said it's a priority area because it's continually
failing our patients in that space.
MR MUSTON: Do I infer from what you said a moment ago --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, the Australian Commission is?
DR PENM: Quality of care.
MR YIK: That's the Australian Commission on Quality and
Safety in Healthcare.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR MUSTON: Do I infer from something you said a moment
ago that the risks associated with that discharge and
transition period are exacerbated in New South Wales by the
fact that it's not a party to the PBS arrangements such
that there is necessarily going to be a very narrow window
within which that transition has to happen and some other
external party will have to engage with whatever the
patient's walked away with and understand it sufficiently
to make sure that the medication that the patient should be
taking continues in the way that it should continue?
MR YIK: Yes, that's right. So because New South Wales
and the ACT government aren't signatories to the
pharmaceutical reform agreements, they are unable to
prescribe and therefore dispense one month's worth of
medicines or the PBS quantities worth of medicines to
patients on discharge.
That is something the New South Wales Government has
been wanting to do and has, I understand, made multiple
representations to the federal government to enact or to
enter into an agreement, so my understanding is that the
ball is in the federal government's court. New South Wales
Government has adopted that policy or that position to want
to have one, but I think it requires the federal government
to support that.

MR MUSTON: Putting to one side whatever financial
benefits or dis-benefits might be associated with entering
into an agreement like that, from a patient's point of view
and the patient safety point of view, giving that period of
a month within which --
MR YIK: Very important.
MR MUSTON: -- follow-up care, primary care givers are
able to see a patient, assess their needs, understand and
make inquiries about the medication, changes in medication
and new medications that might have been introduced, is
important.
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. After an acute admission, you
would have had quite a - you know, often for patients, it
is a major life event to go into hospital because you have
had a heart attack, you have had a stroke, and so those
first few days back at home you are recovering, you're
getting all your life administration all sorted. The last
thing you want to have to think about is, "I'm running out
of medicines in three or five days. Where do I get more?"
This issue is even more pronounced in areas where
there are GP shortages. It's impossible to see a GP within
seven days, so having the ability to have a month's worth
of medicines just gives you that extra time to settle back
at home, take the medicines that you need to have and not
miss any days, because if you are only being given seven
days and you can't see your GP within those seven days,
well, what's going to happen? I think we all know this is
occurring, but this is the reality that we live in.
MR MUSTON: So in terms of that reality, you ask the
rhetorical question, what's going to happen? There would
seem to be two possible answers to that: one is you don't
take the medication that you need to be taking, which has
potentially adverse consequences for the patient?
MR YIK: Absolutely, yes. So you can have a readmission
if you're not taking the right medicine.
A really good example of this, where a patient missed
out on medicine at the transitions of care - so this isn't
really related too much to the pharmaceutical reform
agreement but again it goes to the broader issue around
transitions of care and why you need pharmacists - four

years ago New South Wales had an inquiry into the rural and
regional remote health based off a 60 Minutes story where
a patient was being transferred, I understand, from
a public to a private facility, and they were on a really
important medicine, apixaban, to prevent them from having
another stroke. In that transitions of care there wasn't
a pharmacist providing a service, there wasn't a pharmacist
calling up the private hospital to say, "Hey, this patient
is on apixaban. Please make sure that they are going to
chart that medicine in the private hospital when we hand
them over to your care so that they don't have another
stroke." That medicine was missed, I understand from the
report, by five to seven days and they then later had
a fatal stroke.
So it's these types of issues that are - we know that
they're going to occur before they even occur, because we
know this is what's going to occur. If someone has just
had a stroke, they've been put on these new medicines to
prevent them from having another stroke, it is so important
that they have access to these medicines. But without
a pharmacist at the discharge, at the transitions of care,
no-one is thinking about that. It is no fault against the
nurse or the doctor, but you need a pharmacist whose sole
focus is on those medicines to be the advocate for the
patient so that they have a safe transitions of care.
That issue, you know, without requisite investment
into the pharmacy workforce, it's going to happen again.
I don't know how else to say that, but it's going to happen
again.
In the last four years since that report, where that
inquiry originated from a medicine-related issue, still not
much has really been done to support the funding of
pharmacy departments to make sure that we do have
pharmacists on discharge, at transitions of care, providing
that cognitive and clinical pharmacy service.
MR MUSTON: Not taking the medication that they need is
one possible answer to your rhetorical question. The other
one is, if you can't get into your GP, you will re-present
at the hospital, presumably through emergency, to say,
"I haven't been able to get my medicine. Could you please
give me a script for a little bit more while I wait to see
the GP?"

MR YIK: Yes, and I think that does occur, too. We have
been seeing more and more presentations to EDs because
patients don't have enough medicines, and that can be from,
as you've described, not being given enough on discharge.
There are also obviously other issues around medication
shortages at the moment as well that are also causing some
ED presentations as well.
MR MUSTON: So coming to some of the solutions, I think we
understand the importance of pharmacists within the
hospital setting and the potential challenges that you
identify if there are not sufficient of them from
a pathway - a pipeline point of view, but equally within
the workforce. The first is an increase - you propose an
increase in the number of pharmacy intern positions.
MR YIK: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Perhaps, Dr Penm, you are best placed to
answer this, but could you just explain what is the
intern - what role does an internship play in the career
progression and education of a pharmacist, and what do you
think increasing hospital pharmacy intern positions would
do from a workforce point of view within New South Wales?
DR PENM: Yes. So once a pharmacy student completes their
degree and has a registerable degree, every one of them
needs to complete a one-year internship before they can
practise independently. That comes with both supervised
hours and an exam at the end. So that's every pharmacy
student who has to do that.
At my own university, the University of Sydney, we
have around 350 students coming out every year. As you can
see, we only have 40 hospital internships, which is very
small for the amount that's applying, that's that top
10 per cent, and we have data that 80 per cent of students
want to go to a hospital.
If people don't get that initial entry level into the
hospital - they apply, they don't get it - it definitely
turns them off wanting to come in, but those who do get it
they can see their skills in practice, they get mentorship,
which we know is extremely important in the early years of
development for a healthcare professional, and if you have
a very positive experience early on, that will keep people
for a long time. That's the retention strategy.

But we're finding they're very attracted to hospital
because that's where their medication knowledge will be
used the most, in the most complex patients environment,
but if we don't look after them, then they're going to
leave. So increasing the number will definitely attract
more people to see the joys of hospital, to see - for
patients to get those benefits that we've talked about,
which is really good, and I think we have interns or
students wanting those positions. But we also want to make
sure we look after them once they're in.
MR MUSTON: Looking after them once they're in requires
sufficient workforce to enable mentorship and support to be
provided to the interns, presumably.
DR PENM: Yes. Looking after them is having those
resident training programs afterwards to then facilitate
the specialised skills that they need if they want to
progress their career. It needs to be rewarding them for
those skills and to recognise the value they have - that
comes from the healthcare awards, so that also needs to be
looked at, and then having the educators and mentorship
that we've talked about.
MR MUSTON: Just before we come to the educators and
mentorship again, can I ask, in your statement on page 6
you refer to the situation in Victoria where intern
positions are 60 per cent funded by the state government.
Could I just ask you to expand, does that mean that they
are 40 per cent funded from somewhere else, or they are
not - you only get 60 per cent of an income if you're an
intern?
MR YIK: It is certainly not that we get only 60 per cent
of the wage. In Victoria they have a fairly centralised
recruitment and funding model for hospital pharmacy interns
in Victorian hospitals. That government does take the
entry pipeline into workforce fairly seriously and so the
Victorian government provides 60 per cent of the intern
pharmacist's salary to the hospital and health service, and
so the hospital only has to pay - find 40 per cent of the
intern's wage from their own budget.
In New South Wales, the way that it works is without
that funding, without dedicated funding from the
government, they have to find 100 per cent of the wage, and

that might be the case in other states as well, but I think
the results from Victoria are really clear. They take
entry and workforce pipeline fairly seriously, and they
know that hospitals themselves cannot fund it alone. So
providing that support to Victorian hospitals means that
they can hire even more interns. I think the results speak
for themselves.
DR PENM: One example of that is that one of the largest
hospitals in New South Wales doesn't take any interns.
Even though it's a teaching hospital, it's one of the
largest, in some sense probably needs it the most, they
don't, because it comes 100 per cent out of their budget
and they say, "Well, we're struggling to deliver the
service as it is, we're just going to hire four
pharmacists." The consequence is you're filling in holes
and you're going to cause more problems for yourself in the
future.
MR YIK: In Victoria your major teaching hospitals take
anywhere between 7 to 10 interns each year. I think in
New South Wales it would range from zero to four.
DR PENM: Zero to two. You don't see four very often
these days.
THE COMMISSIONER: What is the hospital you are referring
to in New South Wales?
DR PENM: That would be Westmead Hospital.
MR MUSTON: So do you see value in the centralised
recruitment process which is operated through Victoria?
Putting to one side the way the funding works, of the
salaries, what do you see is the value of that centralised
recruitment process, say starting from the perspective of
the student?
DR PENM: Centralised recruitment would mean that the job
applications are centralised, the whole process of
interviews and putting in your preferences. That comes
with two main benefits. One is it means you can prioritise
all your efforts on making one application good, as opposed
to putting in 40 applications that often have mistakes,
which is very, very exhausting for students.
I see, once they go into a job interview, there will

be over 150 applicants for one position. Their chance of
being rejected is high. But when they get an interview and
they get rejected not just once, they get rejected twice,
three times, four times, they don't want to keep applying.
It's emotionally, mentally exhausting, because it's not
centralised. They've got to apply for each place, and you
can only take so much rejection while doing full-time
study, while also working, making sure exams are okay and
trying to get a job next year, so I find our students would
value a lot from that.
The other part is they have to really prioritise that,
so they can't really say, "I just want this for the
leverage"; it's, "Which hospitals are worth my time?" For
a lot of people based in the general metro region they will
generally go to a large hospital but that means our smaller
regional hospitals suffer for that.
We have people who are probably happy to work there
but they just don't have the capacity to apply for it, they
have to prioritise their time. So we do see in some places
people who will apply to a regional/rural hospital, or they
might want to, but because they are waiting out for the
larger hospital to do their advertisement, they're just not
going to apply until that does. So there are just multiple
add-on effects around distribution and equity of positions
in New South Wales by not having it centralised.
MR MUSTON: Something you said a moment ago about waiting
for a larger hospital to advertise, is it also the case at
the moment in New South Wales that pharmacy positions are
advertised as and when they are required, including intern
positions; there's not a season where everyone who wants
a pharmacist this year puts out an ad and says, "We want
a pharmacist"?
DR PENM: I think they all try to, but the priorities mean
that everyone will start to advertise in the second half of
the year, but that can range -it can be a difference of one
to four months, and every HR group seems to have
a different timeline, you know, how they advertise it. So
we do know we need them for next year, but it's not like
this month they all happen; it can happen in a four- to
six-month period.
MR MUSTON: Do I gather from what you've told us that at
least your view is from the perspective of students, if not

the system, a centralised recruitment process for
pharmacists entering into at least into their intern year
would be a sensible idea?
DR PENM: I think students would love it, would be very
positive towards it.
MR MUSTON: No doubt pharmacists within facilities who are
having to review multiple applications and interview
candidates who they are not going to give the job to would
probably also appreciate it. Mr Yik, as someone who
practices in a hospital perhaps not doing that work, do you
have a comment on that?
MR YIK: I think what Dr Penm has described is very
accurate. It's not just good, as you've described, for the
students but also for the hospital, where they're not
sifting through, you know, more applications than they need
to. So through that central applicant process you can give
your top, you know, three preferences and then you get
matched according to that, so then everyone has less work
to do but it's much more targeted and appropriate and more
efficient for everyone.
MR MUSTON: Increasing the number of intern positions by
100 FTE would have two benefits, presumably: the first is
it would increase the pharmacy workforce at the junior end
who is able to do some of that junior work, like
reconciliation, easy dispensing and the like --
MR YIK: Mmm.
DR PENM: Mmm.
MR MUSTON: -- which would relieve the pressure on
existing pharmacy workforce - yes?
MR YIK: Yes, absolutely. So obviously intern pharmacists
still need to be supervised by pharmacists during their
intern year, but they are able to undertake a lot of those
activities under the supervision of pharmacists that can
contribute to making sure that patients get medication
reconciliation, they get some medication chart review, they
get counselling by a pharmacy professional as well.
MR MUSTON: Whilst there is a burden of the supervision,
by increasing the number of interns you would, in effect,

be increasing the workforce or the realistic workforce -
that is to say, more work could be done by increasing the
number of interns? It's not just that they would be
watching, adding more strain on the resources of existing
pharmacy workforce?
MR YIK: Yes. It certainly does increase the output, the
clinical output that a pharmacy department can provide. It
certainly makes the care more comprehensive and safer and
higher quality as well.
MR MUSTON: From a pipeline point of view, it would seem
logical that increasing the number of intern positions
would improve the strength of the pipeline of pharmacists
coming into hospitals, but is that assumption sound?
MR YIK: Look, it is sound to an extent, because you are
increasing the knowledge base of pharmacy professionals in
New South Wales that are appropriate and trained in the
hospital setting. As we've presented in our evidence,
I think up to - some hospitals are reporting up to
90 per cent of their applicants for hospital pharmacy jobs
are just inappropriate or not suitable or not suitably
qualified for the job, because all of their experience has
been in the community pharmacy setting.
That's transferrable to the hospital setting to an
extent. There's still significant retraining and training
requirements for the hospital setting, and where you are
already a short-staffed workplace, it's a lot to take on,
and so we just end up in this cycle where we end up not
recruiting anyone.
So increasing the number of intern placements can
probably - well, will likely increase the available
workforce pool that is appropriate to work in the hospital
pharmacy setting without significant retraining required,
but I think we also want to keep them in that hospital
setting at the end of their intern year.
We don't want to spend - unfortunately, this is the
case for a lot of states and a lot of hospitals where we
spend a whole year spending money or spending our workforce
on training the intern, our doctors and nurses help train
that intern as well, and then at the end of the year,
"Sorry, there's no funding for your position, even though
we would really like to keep you on this ward, so we're

going to have to let you go back out into the community."
The hospitals rightly train students from all healthcare
disciplines and have a duty to do so, but why are we not
keeping them in the system at the end?
MR MUSTON: In terms of that training and the way in which
it's delivered, you've talked about educators in your
statement and the importance of having a workforce of
educators who actually assist in guiding that training both
at an intern level but also through advanced skills
training. Do you see value in that process being
centralised within the ministry - that is to say, the
training workforce to potentially be a part of, say,
a central pillar of the ministry that's also involved in
recruiting the interns?
MR YIK: Yes, look, I think we're certainly very open to
that. I think at this point we would take any attention or
funding from the ministry that looks at the education and
training of pharmacy professionals beyond internship.
I think as we've described in our evidence, in Australia
there are resident pharmacist and registrar pharmacist
training programs that are convened by AdPha. So far,
we've got over 800 pharmacists who have either undertaken
or have completed a training program, yet only 50 of them -
sorry, less than 50 of them are from New South Wales, and
that is because there is no capacity and no funding to fund
those positions for residents or registrar pharmacists.
Even for hospitals that do want to provide these training
programs and think, "Well, I've got an oncology ward and
I need an oncology pharmacist, I want to train a pharmacist
in the area", again, the lack of educators can often be
a barrier as well.
So even when we want to try and hire education
pharmacists within our hospitals, that can be really
difficult to get approval and clearance from the LHD.
In what you've described, where it's a more
centralised process and you could have pharmacy educators
that are employed by the ministry and deployed to various
LHDs where there is need, I think - I can't speak for all
hospitals, but it would certainly be better than what we
have now, because at the moment, it's quite sparse. The
education pharmacist network in New South Wales is - yes,
it is quite sparse, and so any more funding via various
means would be very, very welcome.

MR MUSTON: That education workforce - you've mentioned
the value, obviously, of face-to-face pharmacy when dealing
with patients as potentially being better than remotely
delivered pharmacy, but remotely is better than nothing.
What about education? Is there scope for remotely
delivered education through pharmacist educators who are
not necessarily on the ground, particularly in smaller
facilities in rural and regional areas?
MR YIK: Yes. I think there absolutely is a capacity for
that and it's something that we would be very, very happy
to explore. As we've talked about, these resident
pharmacists and registrar pharmacist training programs, we
want to deliver them in rural and regional healthcare
settings but, of course, you may not have the education
pharmacists there on site because they don't happen to
live there, but that should not be the
rate-limiting step as to why a young pharmacy professional
can't undertake those training programs.
So we are very open to having mentors or education
pharmacists delivering the services remotely or via, you
know - we all have Zoom and Teams nowadays, and every time
that we accredit those sites to undertake and deliver those
training programs, as long as you can demonstrate that you
can provide that service, then that should be fine. So if
that is to be delivered electronically or via telehealth -
via Zoom or Teams - we would facilitate that and accredit
that program.
MR MUSTON: The ability to know where it's needed and
where that outreach or remote teaching might best be
delivered requires some level of centralised control or
coordination over the process, though, presumably?
MR YIK: It would and it would require the attention and
knowledge of what pharmacy educators provide and the
importance to ensuring the quality of clinical placements
for pharmacy students and for interns and for developing
your current pharmacist workforce as well.
MR MUSTON: In terms of those pharmacists who have
obtained those advanced skills training, you tell us in the
statement - I assume I've understood it correctly - that to
the extent that there are benefits associated with
pharmacists being involved in the delivery of care in terms

of reducing errors, enhancing outcomes, those benefits are
enhanced even further where a pharmacist with some advanced
skills training is operating within an area of that
particular - where they have that skill?
MR YIK: Yes. Absolutely, and we have developed these
programs so that patients are receiving services from the
most appropriately trained pharmacists.
Going back to, you know, two decades ago, if you were
walking into an infectious diseases ward or an oncology
ward, the pharmacist that was being put into that ward may
have just been a general pharmacist who may not have
received training, but because there were just no
formalised training programs at all, there was an
expectation, or it was a standard, really, that you would
just learn on the job.
So you did that model for a number of years, for
decades, because there was no other model to ensure that
pharmacists were ready, educated and prepared, before they
stepped into that ward. And this is what this program aims
to provide, because it's just much safer and more
appropriate for the patient.
MR MUSTON: Given the relatively small number of people in
New South Wales who are passing through this program, do
I infer from what you said a moment ago that, at least in
New South Wales, as distinct, perhaps, from other states,
we're still doing things the same way as we were doing them
decades ago?
MR YIK: If at all, and I guess we go back to our very
early evidence, that there are still many wards that don't
have pharmacists on them at all. But I guess as you've
suggested, even when you do have a pharmacist on that ward
in New South Wales, they may not be the most appropriately
trained or - sorry, they may not have sufficient training
compared to practitioners and their peers in other states.
MR MUSTON: Just in relation to what you tell us about the
resident pharmacist positions and resident training
programs, what is in the context of a pharmacist's
educational and professional journey, a resident position?
Is it a particular assignation of position or is it more
you are a full-time pharmacist working in a facility who
then wants to get some more training?

MR YIK: A resident pharmacist position is aimed at
pharmacists who are entering at the start of their career,
it is to consolidate and expand the skills that they have
obtained in the intern year. For a resident pharmacist in
a hospital, they will often do four six-month rotations, so
it's a two-year program, and those rotations will take them
through the busiest parts of the hospital, so that they go
on a really steep curve in developing and consolidating
their skills.
I think it's six months in the dispensary, six months
in the surgical ward, and six months in a general medicine
ward because both of those wards have really high patient
flows so you get exposed to a lot of different patients and
develop your skills really, really quickly, and
comprehensively.
Then your final rotation can be an area of your choice
that will expose you to a specialist ward. So it could be
your final rotation might be through the oncology ward, it
might be through the psychiatry ward, it might be through
the stroke ward, to get you exposed to an area that you
